question: Is sub-nanosecond latency a physically targetable goal?
answer_per_operation: ALREADY TRUE. One GPU clock cycle is 714 ps, i.e. 0.714 ns. Individual instruction issue is already sub-nanosecond, and across 60 cores the effective per-FLOP time is femtoseconds. There is nothing left to target here.
answer_per_token: PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE by ~6 orders of magnitude. A 1 ns token is 1,000,000,000 tok/s. The binding constraint is bytes moved per token divided by memory bandwidth, and that floor is in MICROseconds.

dispatch_floor.note: A second floor of the same order: the 48-layer dependency chain cannot be collapsed below ~1 Metal dispatch per layer, and dispatch launch latency is ~2-5 us. 48 sequential dispatches is ~100-240 us, comparable to the DRAM floor. Practical floor is therefore ~1 ms/token, i.e. ~1000 tok/s, not the 757 us pure-bandwidth number.

the_real_framing: Q80 currently runs 403,000,000 ns/token against its own 757,074 ns floor. That is 532x above the physical limit. The gap is engineering, not physics - every nanosecond of it is dispatch, host work, occupancy and idle, none of which is bounded below by the machine.
density_is_velocity_quantified: Dropping 4.259241 -> 1.392467 BPW raises the CEILING from 432 to 1321 tok/s, a 3.06x increase in what is physically attainable at all. At 4.259 BPW, 333 TPS (TG3) sits at only 1.30x the floor and would require ~77% of peak bandwidth sustained - not credible. The <=1.5 artifact is what makes the tournament ladder physically reachable, independent of any runtime win.
